explanation: The oath shows what the king claimed — authority over a countess's marriage and service — but one document from one vassal cannot by itself prove how widely or consistently that authority was exercised; royal claims often outran royal enforcement in medieval France.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Latin documents of this kind are routinely and reliably translated by historians.
option_explanations.B: Correct. A single oath demonstrates the king's asserted power over Matilda, but it does not show that such control was standard practice or effectively enforced throughout the kingdom.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Nothing indicates forgery; this is a well-attested type of feudal record.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Written oaths and charters were central instruments of medieval politics.

options: (A) The oath was sworn in Latin, a language modern historians cannot reliably translate.
(B) The oath records the king's demands on a single vassal, not proof that such control was routinely enforced across France.

stem: A historian citing this oath as evidence for the growth of royal power in thirteenth-century France would most need to qualify the claim with which of the following cautions?
stimulus: Let all who see this present letter know that I, Matilda, countess of Nevers, have sworn upon the sacred gospels to my dearest lord Philip, by God's grace the illustrious king of France, that I will do him good and faithful service against all living men and women, and that I will not marry except by his will and grace. To keep these agreements firmly, I have given pledges to the lord king from my own men who were with me, sworn on their oaths, in this manner: that if I should fail to keep these agreements with the lord king — though this shall not be — they are bound to come to the lord king with all their lands and fiefs which they hold from me, and to take their oaths to him against me, until satisfaction has been made to him. — Oath of a French vassal to the king, 1221

explanation: The oath's enforcement mechanism is the point: Matilda's men pledge their own lands and oaths to the king against her, showing how feudal obligation was personal and layered — each link in the chain owed loyalty upward, and the king could activate the lower links against a disloyal vassal.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The pledges show obligation operating in tiers: Matilda owes the king, her men owe her, and the king binds her men directly so they will abandon her if she breaks faith.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Salaried standing armies came later; this oath relies on personal levies and pledged service, not paid troops.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Towns did not choose royal vassals; vassalage was a personal bond between lord and noble.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Fiefs were granted by lay lords, not by the church.

options: (A) Obligations ran in layered chains, so that a vassal's subordinates could be bound to act against the vassal on the lord's behalf.

stem: Musa's account of copper being carried south and exchanged for gold at two-thirds its weight most directly illustrates which of the following?
stimulus: A traveler reported what Sultan Musa of Mali told him: at a certain town the sultan has a copper mine, from which ingots are carried to another town. 'There is nothing in my kingdom,' Musa said, 'on which a duty is levied except this crude copper that is brought in. Duty is collected on this and on nothing else. We send it to the land of the pagan Sudan and sell it for two-thirds of its weight in gold, so that we sell a hundred measures of copper for sixty-six and two-thirds measures of gold.' He added that there are pagan peoples in his kingdom from whom he does not collect the jizya, the tax on non-Muslims, but whom he simply employs in extracting gold from its deposits. The gold is dug from pits about a man's height in depth, found embedded in the sides of the pits or gathered at the bottom. — Al-Umari, Arab historian, writing about 1340

explanation: Musa's hajj — traveling across the Sahara to Mecca with a vast entourage — displayed Mali's wealth and its ruler's membership in the global Muslim community, ties built through the same Saharan trade networks the passage describes.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The pilgrimage was religious and diplomatic, not a military pact against the Mongols.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Islam spread in Mali through trade contacts across the Sahara, not through invasion.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The hajj showed a West African king participating fully in the religious life of the Islamic world, connected to it by the trade routes of the passage.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The 1300s were the height of trans-Saharan trade, not its decline.

options: (A) A formal military alliance between Mali and the Mamluk rulers of Egypt directed against the Mongols.

explanation: Before the cables, orders and prices traveled at the speed of sailing ships. Near-instant messaging let London govern a global empire day by day and let merchants in London react to prices in Bombay the same day — speed became a commercial and political advantage, which is why states and firms invested in the wires.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Speed served both imperial administration and commercial decision-making.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Navies and merchant shipping remained essential; cables carried information, not goods.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Officials were still needed on the ground; the cable made them more, not less, accountable to London.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The network's purpose was imperial and commercial communication, not private correspondence.

The cables ended Britain's need for any ships or navies in Asian waters.
Instant communication made all colonial officials unnecessary.

stem: Columbus's glowing description of Hispana's harbors, rivers, and gold most directly contributed to which of the following?
stimulus: On the island called Hispana there are very lofty and beautiful mountains, rich farms, groves, and fields, most fertile both for cultivation and for pasturage, and well suited for building. The harbors of this island, and the excellence of its rivers in volume and wholesomeness, surpass human belief unless one sees them. Its trees, pasturelands, and fruits differ greatly from those of Juana. Moreover, this Hispana abounds in various kinds of spices, gold, and metals.
